{"id": "00001957-0000-4000-8000-000000001957", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "00001959-0000-4000-8000-000000001959", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a general AWS question about ALB vs NLB rather than something specific to the DevOps Agent product, so I can just answer it directly from my own knowledge without needing tools.\n\n"}]}

{"id": "0000195d-0000-4000-8000-00000000195d", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "The main difference is the network layer each one works at. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic at Layer 7. A Network Load Balancer (NLB) routes TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic at Layer 4.

| | **ALB** | **NLB** |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TLS, TCP_UDP |
| **Routing** | Content-based: host, path, headers, query strings, HTTP method, source IP | Port and protocol only |
| **Performance** | Good, but it inspects each request | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency, and it handles sudden traffic spikes well |
| **IP addresses** | Dynamic IPs, so you use its DNS name | One static IP per Availability Zone, with optional Elastic IPs, and PrivateLink support |
| **Targets** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, and ALBs |
| **Security groups** | Supported | Supported (added in 2023), though some older setups don't use them |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and supports SNI | Can terminate or pass through TLS |
| **Client IP** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header | Preserved at the network level (for instance targets) |
| **Extra features** | Authentication through Cognito or OIDC, WAF integration, redirects, fixed responses, weighted target groups | Works with AWS Global Accelerator and exposes services through PrivateLink |

**When to use an ALB**
- Web apps, microservices, and APIs that need path- or host-based routing, for example `/api/*` to one service and `/app/*` to another.
- Container workloads on ECS or EKS that need several services behind one load balancer.
- Edge features such as WAF, user authentication, or redirects.

**When to use an NLB**
- Non-HTTP protocols such as gaming traffic, IoT, MQTT, or custom TCP/UDP services.
- Workloads that need extreme performance or low latency, or that handle millions of requests per second.
- Cases where clients need fixed IPs to allowlist.
- Exposing a service to other VPCs or accounts through PrivateLink.

You can also put an NLB in front of an ALB. That gives you static IPs or PrivateLink along with Layer 7 routing.

If you'd like, I can look at the load balancers in your account and check which type each one is and how it's configured.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
